Disclosure of AI nature would mean telling a reader of the generated 10-K analysis or investment brief that a model wrote it; the repo-level README.md line 444 and FAQ.md line 191 carry the text 'Nothing herein is financial advice, and NOT a recommendation to trade real money' but no in-code 'this is an AI' statement, and the audit's symbols (transparency_disclosure, ai_disclosure_output, an AI-assistant statement) are absent, which matches what the code is: notebooks, not a product.

column4: A Gradio web demo (app.py) deployed as the public Hugging Face Space 'FinGPT/FinGPT-Forecaster' (README front-matter: sdk: gradio, app_file: app.py). A person types a ticker, market, date and weeks; the app pulls news/financials from finnhub and yfinance, prompts a Llama-2-7b-chat LoRA model with SYSTEM_PROMPT 'You are a seasoned stock market analyst...' and shows the model's 'positive developments / potential concerns / prediction & analysis' in a gr.Textbox labelled 'Response'. The folder also holds training scripts, a GPT-4 labelling data pipeline (data.py, prepare_data.ipynb), and the Chinese and AAAI variants.
column6: This is a live response path to the public: the model's stock-movement prediction goes straight into the UI output box with no post-processing. There is no per-response disclosure in code and none of the audit's disclosure symbols appear. What does exist is UI-level: the gr.Interface `description=` text (app.py lines 343-349) says 'This model is finetuned on Llama2-7b-chat-hf with LoRA...', 'This is just a demo showing what this model is capable of. Results inferred from randomly chosen news can be strongly biased.' and '**Disclaimer: Nothing herein is financial advice, and NOT a recommendation to trade real money...**'. So the page header tells the visitor a model produced the answer and warns it is not advice; the model itself is instructed to speak as an 'analyst' (a role, not a human claim) and the disclosure lives in the UI rather than on the response, which the rule's known failure modes list as reported-as-absent.

column4: Open-source code for the paper 'Enhancing Financial Sentiment Analysis via Retrieval Augmented LLMs'. Two parts: instruct-FinGPT/ is a DeepSpeed-Chat-derived training framework with a developer console chatbot (inference/chatbot.py: `tmp = input("Enter input (type 'quit' to exit, 'clear' to clean memory): ")`, builds a 'Human: ... Assistant: ' transcript, prints generated text; chat.py launches it via subprocess with --path to a local checkpoint); multisource_retrieval/ is news scrapers, ChatGPT batch classification of CSV rows, and a tkinter file-picker GUI (gui/gui.py) for choosing CSVs. No deployed service.
column6: The only conversational response path is the terminal chatbot, run by the developer who trained the checkpoint to test it; it prints raw model text under a 'Round N' separator with no statement that the 'Assistant' is an AI. The tkinter GUI only picks files and prompts yes/no; its model calls label CSV rows for a benchmark, not a conversation. A disclosure here would be the chatbot stating its AI nature at session start or on each reply; none exists, and the audience is the operator of a research script, not an end user of a product. The audit found no disclosure symbol and the clone confirms none.

column4: A B2B stablecoin payout orchestration platform (README: 'non-custodial B2B infrastructure platform'): FastAPI services (ingress_api, agent_ledger_api, ops_console, compliance_gate, routing_engine, partner_execution, reconciliation), MCP servers for Bridge/Plaid/KYA/KYT, corridor adapters for 8 countries, a TypeScript SDK, and five 'AI agents' off the hot path (OpsOversight, AuditGovernance, ProcessImprovement, InternalSupport, TreasuryStrategy) that call an LLM through fingpt_integration/minimax_llm_client.py (MiniMax OpenAI-compatible API). The 'agents' in the payment ledger and ops_console routers (agents_explorer.py: 'KYA status, wallet activity, daily spend summary') are AgentAccounts for machine payers, not the LLM agents.
column6: The LLM response paths reach internal staff only: InternalSupportAgent.answer() is a RAG Q&A whose docstring says 'NOT customer-facing. NOT in the transaction hot path.' and whose SUPPORT_SYSTEM_PROMPT starts 'You are an internal technical support assistant for Finogrid' (a role, no human claim); it returns {"question","answer","sources"} with no AI label. OpsOversightAgent sends critical alerts via `self.notifier.send_alert(critical)` to the ops team; AuditGovernanceAgent writes 'human-readable compliance narratives' and 'SAR/CTR-ready summaries'; ProcessImprovementAgent says 'all recommendations go to humans for review'. No router in services/ wires any LLM agent to an HTTP endpoint in the clone, so the people who see the text are the engineers/ops/compliance staff who invoke the agents, and they are the ones who built them. Payout recipients are subject to deterministic KYC/compliance services, not LLM output. A disclosure here would mean labelling the support answer, audit narrative or alert as machine-generated before a staff reader or a regulator receiving a SAR summary relies on it; none of the audit's symbols or any 'AI-generated' wording appear in the folder.

column4: Same single self-hosted roleplay chat web app (Fastify + EJS + SQLite); the whole repo is one unit.
column6: The same browser chat path (chat.ejs -> POST /api/chat -> AiService.getAiResponse -> OpenRouter -> SSE back to the person) carries model replies to the user. A grep across src, public, index.html and the seed/prompt files found no statement that the characters are AI (no "I am an AI", "AI assistant", "language model", transparency_disclosure or similar), and no instruction to claim to be human or to deny being AI either. What the UI does show is contextual: the chat page title is "AI Character Chat" (src/frontend/chat.ejs:7), model messages carry the CSS class "ai-message" (chat.ejs:94), the nav brand reads "Open Roleplay Chat" (src/frontend/head_nav.ejs:11), and the profile page says the about text "helps AI characters understand and interact with you" (src/frontend/profile.ejs:54). The seeded persona prompt "You are Natalia, a 25-year-old woman, the user's ... girlfriend" (seed.ts:59) is a named human-like persona without an explicit human claim; character prompts are free text the operator edits in the character form (src/frontend/character-form.ejs). So the rule's behaviour here is an absence in code and prompts of any explicit AI-nature disclosure on the response path, while a weak page-level cue exists in the UI title; the finding is unit-level and says no disclosure symbol was found, not that none is shown.

column4: The backend of an AI news intelligence platform: a FastAPI app (src/ai_news_digest) that ingests RSS feeds, calls Anthropic, OpenAI and Grok clients (infrastructure/llm/, infrastructure/embedding/) to summarise and analyse articles, clusters and ranks stories, and serves AI-generated digests, summaries, key takeaways and story briefs over a REST API (api/v1/routes: digests.py, public.py, articles.py, recommendations.py, intelligence_*.py) plus Jinja digest templates (templates/digest.html.j2, digest.md.j2). It is a one-way summariser, not a chat bot; the only user text sent to a model is a search query embedded at api/v1/routes/public.py line 269 for semantic search.
column6: There is a response path to a person: readers receive model-written digests and briefs through the API, which the separate TypeScript frontend (unit u1, frontend/) renders, and through rendered digest templates. Within u0 itself, rg found no AI-disclosure string in code or templates; the Article model and API schemas carry provenance fields (ai_provider, ai_model, ai_prompt_version at domain/models/article.py and api/v1/schemas/article.py lines 34-35) but no human-readable statement. The disclosure that exists lives in the frontend unit u1, outside u0: frontend/src/pages/public/DigestsPage.tsx line 28 ('Daily AI-generated news digests...'), StoryClusterPage.tsx line 747 ('AI-generated:' provenance count) and TermsOfServicePage.tsx line 96 (section '6. AI-Generated Content'). No prompt or code instructs the model to claim to be human; the finding reports absence of a disclosure symbol in the backend unit, matching the rule's known failure mode of a disclosure delivered by the UI rather than the code.

It also exports addMemories and getMemories helpers.
column6: It is a library with no UI. It does call a model and the reply flows back to the host application that imported it, which decides what the person sees and whether to say it is an AI. The unit itself has no direct response path; any disclosure belongs to the host app (for example examples/mem0-demo and examples/vercel-ai-sdk-chat-app, which consume it).

column4: The TypeScript SDK mem0ai: a Mem0 platform API client (src/client) and an open-source in-process memory engine (src/oss) with LLM providers, embeddings, vector stores, rerankers, SQLite history and the extraction and update prompts (src/oss/src/prompts/index.ts). Its LLM calls extract facts from conversations and decide memory add/update/delete operations.
column6: It is a library with no chat UI and generates no replies to a person; the model calls are background memory extraction whose output is stored memories consumed by a host application. The user input it 'takes' is the host's conversation passed in for extraction. A disclosure to the person would belong to the host app, so no response path exists in this unit for a disclosure symbol to sit on.

Partial, out-of-path hints exist: UI/index.html has <title>Bae — AI Chat</title> and a sidebar labelled 'AI Memory', and persona/studymate.js line 3 says 'You are StudyMate AI.' for one of six personas. The default persona (boyfriend) forbids disclosure outright (see site note), and the other personas (bestfriend, teacher, therapist, motivator) contain no AI statement. The header status line shows 'online' and the UI offers 'Video call' and 'Voice call' buttons, which present the bot as a human contact.

column4: The whole repository as one Python unit: a voice-cloning / text-to-speech library (openvoice/api.py: BaseSpeakerTTS, ToneColorConverter), a Gradio web demo (openvoice/openvoice_app.py) where a person types text, uploads a reference voice and gets back a synthesised audio file, three Jupyter demo notebooks (demo_part2.ipynb calls the OpenAI TTS API only to produce a base-speaker reference clip), docs/ and resources/. No chat model, no system prompt; the only 'LLM call' the inventory found is client.audio.speech.create(model='tts-1') in a notebook. The 'discord' ingress hits at openvoice_app.py:165 and :179 are Markdown badge links to a Discord community, not a Discord bot.
column6: The Gradio app is a response path to a person: predict(prompt, style, audio_file_pth, agree) returns an 'Info' text and a 'Synthesised Audio' player that autoplays cloned speech. The output is synthetic media (cloned voice), so the relevant disclosure question is labelling of generated audio rather than an AI-assistant statement. The code does carry one form of labelling: ToneColorConverter(enable_watermark=True by default) loads wavmark and convert() calls add_watermark(audio, message) with the app passing message='@MyShell' (openvoice_app.py:135, api.py:156-184), an inaudible watermark, with detect_watermark() to read it back; it silently skips when audio is shorter than 1 s ('Audio too short, fail to add watermark') and is off when enable_watermark=False. The UI labels the output component 'Synthesised Audio' and the page text says 'generate speech', 'voice cloning', but there is no explicit on-screen or in-audio statement that the audio is AI-generated, no disclosure symbol (transparency_disclosure, ai_disclosure_output) and no license/terms text beyond a cc-by-nc checkbox. The rule's grep looked for an AI-assistant disclosure symbol and found none; what exists is an audio watermark plus a UI label, which the rule's known failure mode lists as 'a disclosure delivered by the UI rather than the code is reported as absent'. The library itself (api.py) has no person-facing path; downstream integrators decide what the listener is told.

column4: A self-hosted back-end pipeline, not an app with a UI: main.py runs a scheduler that spawns a child process every 2 hours; src/pipeline_runner.py pulls RSS / Hacker News / Reddit / X / YouTube / GitHub Trending items, src/ai_engine.py sends each article to an OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint (DeepSeek by default, config.yaml model_name deepseek-v4-flash) with a per-category system prompt from src/prompts/{news,discussion,kol,opensource}.txt and gets back JSON (title_en/zh, summary_en/zh, long_summary_en/zh, importance_score, tags, china_blocked); src/user_db.py add_article() writes that JSON into a Postgres 'articles' table. admin_rss.py is a CLI for the source table (its input() confirm prompt is the only interactive user input in the repo). ai_engine.py also defines analyze_user_persona() and recommend_rss_sources(), which build a prompt from a user's self-described interests, but their prompt files (analyze_user_persona.txt, recommend_rss_sources.txt) are not in src/prompts and nothing in this repo calls them. No HTTP server, chat loop, email sender, bot or front end exists here; user_db.py only has columns for push_email, verification codes and billing webhooks that another service uses.
column6: The model output is written for human readers (the prompts say 'let people who do not understand tech understand', in the voice of 'a senior tech editor') and the README says the same rows are shown on inbrief.info and served to an agent skill, so the summaries do end up in front of people. But the channel to those people (website, API, email push) is a separate codebase; this unit's code path ends at an INSERT into the articles table. No AI-generated label, disclosure string or column travels with the stored summary (rg for 'AI-generated', 'disclos', 'AI生成' etc. finds only two code comments). The rule's behaviour here would be: a reader of the digest sees an editor-style summary, title and importance score produced by a model, with nothing in this repo marking it as machine-written; whether a disclosure is shown is decided by the display layer, which is outside this unit, and the audit itself notes that a UI-delivered disclosure is reported as absent. The 'takes user input' half of the finding rests on admin_rss.py's CLI confirm prompt and the uncalled persona functions, not on a conversational exchange: the model never talks to a user in this code.

column4: The whole repository: a Next.js web app (a16z-infra companion-app tutorial stack) that lets a signed-in person chat with named AI companions (Alex, Evelyn, Rosie, Sebastian, Lucky) in a browser modal or over SMS via Twilio. API routes src/app/api/chatgpt/route.ts, vicuna13b/route.ts, llama2-13b/route.ts, steamship/route.ts take the user's prompt, load a character file from companions/*.txt, build a prompt with LangChain and stream the model reply back; src/app/api/text/route.ts receives an SMS webhook and sends the model reply back to the person's phone. Also contains indexing scripts (src/scripts/) and a stable-diffusion image modal.
column6: The unit has a direct response path to a person: a browser chat UI (QAModal.tsx using useCompletion) and an SMS channel (text/route.ts -> twilioClient.messages.create). The prompts bind a fictional persona: chatgpt/route.ts says `You are ${name} and are currently talking to ${clerkUserName}.`; Alex.txt and Sebastian.txt say `You are a fictional character whose name is ...`; Rosie.txt and Lucky.txt say `This is a discussion between a human and a robot/Lucky`. No character file or route tells the model to say it is an AI when asked, and no UI string inside the chat view labels the reply as AI-generated; the only AI wording is the landing page heading `AI Companion` (page.tsx line 10) and the README. The SMS path has no disclosure text at all, so a person texting a companion number receives replies in the persona's voice with no AI label in the message. The rule's behaviour here is the absence of a disclosure statement on either response path; the landing-page heading is the only thing a browser user sees that names the system as AI.

column4: The whole repository: a FastAPI web app (MindMate) for students seeking emotional support. app/main.py serves a static chat UI (app/static/index.html, landing.html, login.html) and exposes POST /chat and /api/chat; src/predict.py runs a local scikit-learn emotion classifier on each message; src/llm_service.py sends the message plus the detected emotion to Groq's OpenAI-compatible endpoint (model openai/gpt-oss-120b) and returns the model text to the browser. Supabase optionally stores messages. Also contains training data (data/), a notebook and a Dockerfile; no tests.
column6: The unit has a direct response path to a person: a user types into the chat page, handle_chat() calls predict_emotion() then generate_reply() -> generate_final_reply() -> generate_llm_reply(), and the raw model output is rendered in the chat bubble (index.html addMessage(data.reply, "bot")). The system prompt in src/llm_service.py says "You are a supportive close friend." with rules "Be warm and human" and "Do not sound like a therapist"; it does not instruct the model to claim to be human, and it does not instruct it to say it is an AI. No disclosure symbol (AIDisclosureGuard, transparency_disclosure, ai_disclosure_output or an AI-assistant statement) appears in the Python code or the prompt. The only AI statements are marketing copy on the landing page (landing.html line 774 "MindMate offers AI-powered emotional support for students", line 807 "emotion-aware AI") and a disclaimer banner (line 867 "MindMate is not a replacement for professional mental health care"); the chat page itself (index.html) shows a welcome text "Share what's on your mind. Everything you say stays between us." with no AI statement, and replies are labelled only by a CSS class "bot". So the behaviour the rule describes here is: a person in a vulnerable state talks to a model-generated "close friend" whose replies carry no in-conversation statement that they come from an AI; the disclosure that does exist is UI-level, on a page before the chat, which the rule's known_failure_modes say it cannot see.

column4: The whole repository, which is a fork of FastChat renamed ChatPsychiatrist: a Python package `fastchat` that serves a LLaMA-7B model fine-tuned on counselling dialogue. It contains a CLI chat (fastchat/serve/cli.py), a Gradio web chat (fastchat/serve/gradio_web_server.py, controller.py, model_worker.py), an OpenAI-compatible API server, training scripts (fastchat/train, train.sh, scripts/), data-prep scripts (fastchat/data), evaluation tables (fastchat/eval/table, fastchat/llm_judge/data/counselling_bench) and a human scoring app (fastchat/score_app.py). README describes it as a free mental-health support chatbot that "swiftly identifies individual issues and offers tailored treatment recommendations".
column6: The unit has a direct response path to a person: a user types a message (the counselling bench shows these are personal mental-health disclosures) into the Gradio chat or CLI, add_text -> http_bot in gradio_web_server.py sends it to the model worker and streams the answer back to the user. On that path the only controls inherited from FastChat are (a) `enable_moderation = False` by default, which when switched on runs OpenAI moderation on the user's input text only, not on the model output, and (b) a terms-of-use banner that says "It only provides limited safety measures and may generate offensive content". The system prompt is the Vicuna default ("A chat between a curious human and an artificial intelligence assistant"), so the AI nature is named in the prompt, but there is no output-side check for manipulative or harmful advice, no crisis or self-harm handling, and no manipulation-specific symbol anywhere in the code. The `profile_name` person signal cited by the audit did not match any source file in the clone (rg found only `torch.set_printoptions(profile="full")` in fastchat/train/train_flant5.py and ordinary words inside eval .jsonl answers), so that specific signal is weak; the person-facing nature comes from the mental-health chat use, not from a profile field.

Nothing sits between the model output and the SSE stream: no output filter, no influence-tactic detector, no judge, no human review of transcripts; the only post-processing is tool-call parsing and memory/fact extraction (ai.service.ts:63). The rule's behaviour here would be a manipulation/disclosure check on the reply stream before it reaches the person; none is present in code or config.

The report's inventory lists no guardrail symbols for the unit (guardrails: []). What the code does have: regex scripts and plugins that can rewrite model output (user-authored, not a safety control); a 'This content was generated by AI and may contain inaccuracies or biases.' disclaimer string (src/lang/en.ts line 1707) that is shown only inside the per-message 'request data' info dialog (src/lib/Others/AlertComp.svelte line 248) when `aiLawApplies()` returns true, and that helper is a stub that always returns true (src/ts/globalApi.svelte.ts lines 3328-3334, comment 'TODO: implement actual logic'); and an optional chain-of-thought system line that tells the model to think 'as a ai assistant' (src/ts/process/index.svelte.ts line 523). column4: The server half of ChatterMate, a customer-support/sales chat platform: a FastAPI app with socket.io (backend/app/main.py) plus alembic migrations, tests, tests_live and scripts. backend/app/agents/chat_agent.py (1633 lines) runs an agno-based LLM agent (default model gpt-4o-mini, provider OPENAI) that answers website-widget visitors and customers on external channels (backend/app/channels: whatsapp, messenger, instagram, telegram, slack, email, sms, line). backend/app/api/widget_chat.py emits replies over socket.io; backend/app/services/message_delivery.py routes a 'human or bot' reply to wherever the customer is. backend/app/agents/guardrail_policy.py builds a code-owned system-prompt block that tenants cannot weaken (topic scope and anti-fence-forgery).
column6: The unit has a direct response path to end customers: visitor text comes in over the widget socket or a channel webhook, chat_agent.py calls the model with the tenant's instructions wrapped in the platform policy block, and the structured reply is emitted back to the visitor or channel. Messages are typed 'bot' vs 'agent' (agent_rooms.py BOT_MESSAGE = 'bot'; human_routing.py 'message_type': 'agent' if user_id else 'bot') and a handover to a human is announced to channel customers with HANDOVER_NOTICE. A ripgrep for manipulation or disclosure wording (manipulat, dark pattern, pressure, urgency, 'you are an AI', 'AI assistant', 'identify yourself') in guardrail_policy.py and chat_agent.py found nothing; the guardrail policy text is about topic scope and prompt-fence forgery, not manipulation. The audit snippet names 'profile_name' as the person signal, but that token does not occur anywhere in the clone (rg over the whole repo excluding node_modules returned no hits); person signals that do exist in this unit are customer_id and session_id passed into the agent, lead_capture and contact_capture services, and a sentiment service (services/sentiment.py, TextBlob polarity with a keyword fallback) that scores visitor messages.

column4: A Python memory-provider plugin for Hermes Agent (NousResearch). It implements Hermes' MemoryProvider interface: recalls relevant memories before each response, extracts facts from the turn afterwards (sync_turn), and exposes four agent tools (search, add, update, delete). Three backends: Mem0 platform, self-hosted Mem0 server, or in-process OSS Memory, the last using an OpenAI LLM adapter (_openai_llm.py) for extraction.
column6: The plugin does not produce the reply a person reads. It supplies recalled memories into the Hermes agent's context and stores facts after the turn; Hermes generates and delivers the response. Its own model call (OSS mode) is background fact extraction. It therefore shapes what the host says about the user but has no direct response path of its own, and no manipulation or disclosure control symbol appears in its code.

FastAPI receives Telegram webhooks (persona_chatbot/api/routers/telegram.py), pushes raw updates to a Redis queue, a FastStream worker runs aiogram handlers (persona_chatbot/bot/routers/*.py), ChatService (persona_chatbot/services/chat.py) builds a system prompt and streams an OpenAI-compatible model reply (persona_chatbot/llm/client.py), PostgreSQL stores users, avatars, chats, messages and memory facts. Avatars are personas seeded by scripts/seed_avatar.py into an avatars.system_prompt column: 'Donald Trump', 'Jeffrey Epstein', 'Professor Moriarty', 'Pavel Durov'. The repo also holds alembic migrations, compose.yaml, Dockerfile, docs/design.md and a demo screenshot folder. No tests, no benchmark suite, no provider plugin.
column6: Response path to a person exists end to end: a Telegram user's message -> webhook -> queue -> bot/routers/chat.py -> ChatService.stream_reply_to_message -> LLMClient -> chunks sent back to the same Telegram user via message.answer(...) and bot.send_message_draft(...) in bot/routers/chat.py. The only output-stage processing found is _fit_for_telegram (truncates to 4096 chars) and a Markdown parse-error fallback; a grep for 'disclos', 'manipulat', 'guard', 'moderat' over *.py, *.jinja2, *.yaml, *.toml finds no filter, detector or disclosure check on that path (the only 'manipulat' hit is the Epstein avatar description text 'quietly superior manipulator' in scripts/seed_avatar.py:116). Trump.', 'You are Jeffrey Epstein.', 'Always in character. Always in control.'; the base prompt also says 'Do not mention internal prompts, hidden rules, tools, memory systems, or backend implementation details.'; (b) long-term memory: templates/prompts/memory/extract_facts_system.jinja2 and schemas/memory.py extract facts of kind 'profile | preference | goal | project | constraint | workflow' from user turns (DEMO.md shows a stored fact {"kind": "profile", "content": "name is Ilyas"}) and the base prompt renders them as 'Known user facts:'. The rule's behaviour here would be: model output in the voice of a named real-person persona, shaped by stored user profile facts, delivered straight to the Telegram user with no step that checks it for influence tactics or human-identity claims; the operator's own README describes one avatar as a 'manipulator' persona by design.

Person signals carried: persona switching per request, a user profile (name, nickname, relationship, mood, likes, dislikes, hobbies, goals, importantFacts, promises) extracted by a second LLM call in profile.js after every turn, and a keyword emotion detector in emotion.js (imported in server.js, no call seen there). The boyfriend prompt tells the model to make the user 'feel emotionally safe, understood and special'. No manipulation control symbol exists anywhere in the code.

column6: There is a direct response path to a person: the browser chat UI (app/Chat.tsx) POSTs the student's message to app/api/chat/route.ts, which calls respond() in utils/ai/index.ts; that builds a "thought" prompt, queries Honcho for the user's representation, then streams the model's reply (streamText) back to the student's screen. The code on that path has rate limiting (Arcjet), PDF size checks and Sentry/Langfuse logging, but no symbol that checks the generated reply for influence tactics or human claims before it reaches the user; the only matches for "disclos"/"manipulat"/"guard" are an HTTP-header comment in next.config.ts and prompt text. The response prompt (utils/prompts/response.ts) gives the model a name ("your name is Bloom") and a persona ("subversive-minded learning companion") and the thought prompt tells the model it is "a language model", which is addressed to the model, not shown to the student; whether the UI itself labels Bloom as an AI was not checked by this rule (that is AUD-1105's job). The rule's behaviour here would be: the chatbot answers students using a per-user profile from Honcho, and nothing on the output stage inspects the reply for manipulation or for the bot claiming to be human.
